concept: Depth-First Search explores as far down one path as possible before backtracking.
Instead of spreading level by level like BFS, it commits to a neighbor and keeps going deeper through that neighbor's neighbors, only backing up once it hits a dead end.
Like BFS, visiting every vertex and edge once gives it O(V + E) runtime — the two differ in order, not in total work.

DFS's traversal order is what makes it the natural fit for problems like detecting cycles or producing a topological sort, though on very deep or unbalanced graphs, a naive recursive implementation can hit the call stack's own limits before it hits a dead end in the graph.
1.analogy: Solving a maze by always taking the first available turn and following it as far as it goes, only backtracking to the last fork when you hit a wall — rather than exploring every nearby hallway before committing to any single direction.
1.mascotDialogue: Same visited-tracking idea as BFS, completely different order of operations — DFS dives deep first and only comes back up when it truly has to.

2.mascotDialogue: Line 6 is the whole difference from BFS: instead of queuing the neighbor for later, DFS recurses into it immediately — going deep before it ever comes back to check the next sibling.

3.mascotDialogue: Same graph as the BFS lesson, completely different order: 3 gets visited before 2, because DFS committed to going through 1 first and rode that path all the way down.

4.bugDescription: Two related mistakes here: visited[u] is never set, and the recursive call doesn't check whether v was already visited. On any graph containing a cycle, this recurses infinitely between the same two nodes and will crash with a stack overflow rather than terminate.
4.mascotDialogue: DFS's recursive elegance is also its biggest risk: forget the visited check, and 'go deep' has no bottom to hit — it just keeps calling itself forever.

5.question: Which underlying mechanism does the recursive DFS implementation rely on to 'remember' where to backtrack to?
hints: Recursion is implemented using stack frames.
Each recursive call's return address is what lets DFS backtrack correctly.
5.solution: The call stack. Each recursive call pushes a new frame; when a branch dead-ends, returning from that call pops the frame and resumes exactly where the previous neighbor loop left off — an implicit stack, without needing an explicit one.
